question: Assume today is 2026-09-10. You know nothing published after this date. Estimate the total container volume handled by the Port of Los Angeles in September 2026, in TEUs (twenty-foot equivalent units; loaded and empty imports and exports combined), as it will be first reported in the Port of Los Angeles's monthly cargo news release.

target.what: Total container throughput handled by the Port of Los Angeles in September 2026, reported as TEUs and combining loaded and empty imports and exports, as first published in the Port of Los Angeles monthly cargo news release.
target.publisher: Port of Los Angeles (monthly cargo news release)
target.cadence: Monthly; prior-month cargo statistics are typically released in the following month's cargo news release
target.caveats: The target period is future/ongoing relative to the 2026-09-10 cutoff: only September 1-10 has elapsed and the September 2026 actual is not available. The first-reported monthly total may later be revised. TEUs are throughput counts aggregated across loaded imports, loaded exports, empty imports, an

candidates.perspective: Port of Los Angeles time-series analyst
candidates.hypothesis: September 2026 total TEU is best anchored by recent monthly totals and repeated September seasonal ratios. If the 2026 run-rate and seasonal pattern remain stable, a September seasonal factor applied to the latest available run-rate narrows the estimate. Main transfer assumption: no definitional break in TEU accounting and no extraordinary September shock.
candidates.data_to_find: Port of Los Angeles monthly total TEUs and loaded/empty import/export components for September in earlier years and for 2026 months published on or before 2026-09-10; same-period year-over-year changes; any revisions. Minimum evidence: at least several September observations plus the latest 2026 monthly total. Substitute: year-to-date 2026 TEUs and monthly index.
search_hints: Port of Los Angeles monthly cargo September 2025 total TEUs
Port of Los Angeles cargo statistics August 2026 TEUs
Port of Los Angeles TEU monthly history

candidates.hypothesis: LA throughput can be bridged from San Pedro Bay combined throughput multiplied by LA's share. If LA's share of the adjacent port complex is stable around recent values, an independent forecast or early indicator for Long Beach/San Pedro Bay constrains September 2026. Transfer assumption: adjacent ports face similar regional trade and carrier service rotations, though share can shift with service strings.
candidates.data_to_find: Port of Long Beach monthly TEUs for September in earlier years and 2026 year-to-date; combined San Pedro Bay container totals if published; monthly LA share of the complex; any September 2026 schedule or forecast for Long Beach. Substitute: West Coast port totals and LA share.
search_hints: Port of Long Beach monthly cargo September 2025 TEUs
San Pedro Bay container throughput August 2026
Los Angeles Long Beach port market share TEU

candidates.hypothesis: Monthly throughput equals scheduled container-vessel calls times average TEU exchange per call, adjusted for omitted or missed calls. September 2026 vessel arrival schedules and service strings observed before or during the month provide an independent exposure measure. Transfer assumption: average moves per call from recent months by vessel class or service remains applicable.
candidates.data_to_find: Port of Los Angeles container-vessel arrival schedule for September 2026, terminal berth schedules, service strings, vessel capacities, and expected calls; recent monthly TEUs divided by container-vessel calls to derive average exchange per call. Minimum evidence: count and capacity of scheduled calls.
search_hints: Port of Los Angeles vessel arrival schedule September 2026 container
Los Angeles container terminal berth schedule September 2026
Port of Los Angeles container vessel calls 2026

candidates.hypothesis: Realized throughput is bounded by terminal and berth capacity times utilization and operating days. If September schedules imply near-normal utilization, the capacity route checks plausibility and sets a ceiling or floor. Transfer assumption: publicly known terminal capacity and utilization are reasonably representative of realized container moves.
candidates.data_to_find: Terminal container capacity in TEU per year or moves per hour, berth length and crane count, gate and rail capacity, planned operating hours, berth occupancy or utilization for September 2026, and labor shifts. Substitute: historical peak monthly throughput as a practical capacity bound.

candidates.hypothesis: Published port or trade forecasts for 2026 and national container-import forecasts can be converted to September LA TEUs via LA share and monthly seasonality. Forecast error and policy changes are the main uncertainties. Transfer assumption: forecast coverage and definitions match Port of Los Angeles total TEUs after adjustment.
candidates.data_to_find: Port of Los Angeles budget or forecast for fiscal year 2026/2027 with monthly or quarterly TEU guidance; national US container-import forecasts for September 2026 from sources such as NRF Global Port Tracker, Drewry, BIMCO, or carriers; LA share of national imports. Need forecasts dated on or before 2026-09-10.

candidates.hypothesis: Advance manifest, ISF, booking, or port-community-system counts for containers moving through Los Angeles in September 2026 provide an early physical-flow count. Conversion from bookings or manifests to TEUs requires cancellation/no-show and empty-container adjustments; at the cutoff, only partial-month data may exist.
candidates.data_to_find: Container bookings, advance manifests, or ISF filings for Los Angeles ports for September 2026; weekly loaded import and export container counts; cancellation rates; empty repositioning. Substitute: carrier booking indices or port-community weekly volumes.
search_hints: Los Angeles port advance manifest container bookings September 2026
Port of Los Angeles weekly container volume September 2026
San Pedro Bay container bookings TEU

candidates.hypothesis: Tariff changes, port labor actions, carrier blank sailings, canal or Red Sea diversions, and calendar effects can shift September 2026 away from seasonal history. Measure exposure via announced blank sailings, service changes, and policy effective dates before the cutoff; use these as scenario adjustments to baseline routes, not as a direct estimate.
candidates.data_to_find: Announced transpacific blank sailings and service suspensions for September 2026; US tariff effective dates and covered product shares; port labor or weather disruptions; Labor Day calendar effect; carrier routing changes. Need dates and affected capacity where possible.

candidates.hypothesis: Total TEU equals loaded imports plus loaded exports plus empty imports plus empty exports. Forecasting loaded imports from national import demand and LA share, with exports and empties from recent ratios, reduces reliance on total-seasonality assumptions. Transfer assumption: component shares and empty-repositioning ratios remain near recent ranges.

assessment.note: Single release, one measurement: July 2026 total (960,464), July 2025 total (1,019,837) and the -5.82% YoY change are internally consistent restatements of the same table. They are not three independent signals; the YoY figure is a derived ratio, not a separate observation.

July 2026 component rows (loaded imports, loaded exports, total loaded, total empty) sum arithmetically to the July 2026 total, and p8 supplies the July 2025 empty level. Same source and same table, so this corroborates internal consistency rather than independent measurement. Key structural fact: in July 2026 loaded imports fell about 8%, loaded exports about 8%, and empties only about 1.5% — the total decline is broad-based, not an empties artefact.
Cumulative Jan-Jul 2026 (6,083,067) vs Jan-Jul 2025 (5,975,649) and the stated +1.80% agree; again one measurement restated three ways.

Not a contradiction but a material tension: a positive year-to-date change through July coexisting with a -5.82% July means the year ran stronger earlier and decelerated in the most recent month. This is the central judgement for September 2026 — whether the July dip is noise (favour the YTD signal, m3) or the start of a downshift (favour the July signal, m2).
Annual series 2023-2025 from the same publisher; p60 is a duplicate of p12 from a different snapshot. Establishes the ~10.2-10.3M TEU annual scale used only as context and for share arithmetic.

All from the same October 2024 release. Q3 2024 is nested inside the January-September 2024 cumulative, so these are not independent; the September 2024 record is partly a tariff/port-strike front-loading month, which makes it a poor 'normal' seasonal analogue.

methods.rationale: Persistence baseline: use the most recent same-month actual, September 2025 (p50 = 883,053 TEUs). Justification is that 2026 has run close to 2025 on a year-to-date basis (+1.80%, p11), so a flat same-month carry-forward is the minimal-assumption anchor. It deliberately ignores the July 2026 dip (p3), so it defines the upper side of the plausible range when treated together with m2. Shared failure mode: a genuine level shift in H2 2026 (tariff timing, service changes) is invisible to it.

Transfers the freshest monthly year-over-year change onto the same-month base: September 2025 total scaled by July 2026 / July 2025 (p1 / p2). July 2026 is the last published month before the 2026-09-10 cutoff, so this is the most current monthly momentum available. Transfer assumption: the July year-over-year rate (a broad-based ~6% decline across loaded imports, loaded exports and empties) persists into September rather than being a single-month timing artefact. Failure mode: if the July dip was an arrival-calendar or single-string effect, this method understates. Note it shares its base (p50) with m1 and m4, so agreement among these three is not independent confirmation of the level.

p11.role: Port of Los Angeles calendar-year 2026 year-to-date (January-July) total TEU year-over-year change, used as the growth increment from September 2025 to September 2026

methods.rationale: Same-month base scaled by the 2026 year-to-date growth rate: the assumption is that September 2026 tracks the year's cumulative trend (+1.80%, p11) and that the July dip (p3) is transitory. This is the natural counterpart to m2 and brackets the persistence assumption from above. Failure mode: the YTD signal is stale by two months (August and September 2026 unobserved), so a mid-year turning point makes it biased high. Shares the p50 base with m1, m2, m4.

methods.rationale: Judgement-weighted same-month transfer, explicitly acknowledging that the two kept 2026 signals point in opposite directions and that one month cannot settle which dominates. Central value sits between the July-momentum route (m2) and the YTD route (m3), with a 10-90 band wide enough to cover both signals plus month-boundary arrival noise. Failure mode: it is an explicit assumption rather than a measured quantity, and it is anchored on a base month (September 2025) that was itself depressed relative to 2024, so a rebound scenario is represented only through the upper tail. Correlated with m1, m2, m3 through p50.

assumptions.name: September 2026 vs September 2025 total TEU change factor, Port of Los Angeles
assumptions.rationale: Bounded by the two observed 2026 signals: calendar-year-to-date growth of +1.80% through July (p11), which if sustained implies roughly flat-to-up, and the July 2026 monthly change of -5.82% (p3), which if sustained implies a mid-single-digit decline. The July decline was broad-based across loaded imports, loaded exports and empties (p4, p5, p7), which argues against treating it as a pure month-boundary artefact, but one month is thin evidence and the 2025 autumn months already trended down, so a partial fade of the July drop is assumed. The value is placed slightly below flat, closer to the recent month than to the YTD signal, because monthly momentum dominates for adjacent-month transfers; the 10-90 band spans the full range implied by the two signals plus arrival-timing noise of several percent per month. Independent secondary evidence (elevated but flat-to-falling spot rates, p27, p30) is too ambiguous to shift the central value.
assumptions.applies_when: The 2026 accounting definition of total TEU (loaded + empty, import + export) is unchanged, no port labour action, tariff-effective-date surge or major service-string change disrupts September 2026, and arrival timing noise around the month boundary stays within historical bounds.
assumptions.falsified_by: Evidence that August/early-September 2026 volumes rebounded strongly (e.g. an August 2026 monthly print well above July's, or scheduled September 2026 Transpacific capacity at or above 2025 levels), or conversely evidence of a new tariff deadline or labour disruption pulling volume sharply down in September 2026.

assessment.note: Single Port of Los Angeles July 2026/July 2025 release. p3 is the derived p1/p2 change; p4+p5 approximates p6; p6+p7 approximates p1; p7 vs p8 shows empties nearly flat. Internally consistent accounting, but these are one source, not independent confirmation.
Year-to-date Jan-Jul 2026 and 2025 totals in the same release; p11 (+1.8%) is p9/p10. Same source as the monthly figures, so it corroborates the YTD trend but adds no independent measurement.

Jan/Feb 2026 component rows sum to the monthly totals and to the cumulative total; the near-zero 'empty imports' column recurs in p48, so it is a consistent reporting convention, not a typo in one cell. Used only as component-share evidence, not as a level for September.
September 2025 components sum to p50. This is the key base period for any September 2026 year-over-year route; loaded imports are ~52% of the total, empties ~35%.

September 2024 record release; components p20+p22+p24 sum to p15. Shows September has repeatedly been a strong month (record 2024), which is why 2024-2025 September values, not an average of older years, should anchor the seasonal level.

Aug/Oct 2025 monthly components and 2025 annual totals; p60 and p12 are the same 2025 annual total. Implied annual empty imports are negligible, consistent with p32/p37/p48. Same publisher throughout.

Secondary-source monthly context (June 2025 892k, Dec 2025 792k, July 2025 up 8.5% YoY, July 2025 'one million TEUs'). These restate the port's own numbers, so they are context and a plausibility check, not independent evidence; p67 is a rounded restatement of exact p2.

Freight-rate context as of late Aug 2026: WCI near $4,473/FEU, roughly flat week-on-week, still 111% above a year earlier. High spot rates with flat momentum are consistent with soft-but-not-collapsing transpacific liftings; use as directional context for the year-over-year change factor, not as a level input.

Tension within the kept evidence: YTD 2026 is +1.8% (p11) while July 2026 is -5.82% YoY (p3) with loaded imports -8.12%. Either the early-2026 strength is fading in H2, or July was noise/frontloading payback. This disagreement is exactly what the assumption range for the September 2026 change factor must straddle.

assumptions.rationale: Anchored on kept evidence: YTD 2026 is +1.8% (p11) but July 2026 was -5.82% YoY (p3) with loaded imports -8.12% (p4 vs its 2025 row), implying the early-2026 strength is fading in H2 as frontloaded/tariff-driven volumes normalize. Best estimate for Port of Los Angeles total container throughput (loaded and empty imports plus exports combined) in September 2026 is 869,468 TEU (80% model-based interval 631,119 to 1,197,834 TEU). The combination averages 4 methods at equal weights: 883,053 TEU (25%), 831,644 TEU (25%), 900,286 TEU (25%), and 864,392 TEU (25%). All four rest on the observed September 2025 base of 883,053 TEUs; m2 applies the July 2025-to-July 2026 change (1,019,837 TEUs to 960,464 TEUs), m3 carries the observed YTD growth of 1.8%, and m4 applies an assumed change factor of 0.98 (range 0.876 to 1.095). Only the historical points are observed; the September 2026 level is a transfer or assumption. The interval is conditional, not a demonstrated accuracy guarantee. The main risk is a September-specific shock, since July 2026 already fell year-over-year. Actual September 2026 data would most improve the estimate.

Key assumptions (proposed by the analyst model, not observed; code samples each one between the bounds shown):
- a1 September 2026 vs September 2025 total TEU change factor, Port of Los Angeles: 0.98 ratio, range 0.876 to 1.095 (range widened by code); used by m4. Overturned by: Evidence of sharply stronger September 2026 bookings/gate moves (e.g. a renewed pre-tariff pull-forward or sustained double-digit YoY gains in weekly volumes), or of major terminal disruption, labor action, or mass blank sailings that would push the outcome outside the stated range.

by_construction: Only URLs leave the searcher (code regex); extractor, judge and final prompts never contain search result titles, snippets or the searcher's text. This holds by construction and is not measured.
residual_risks: The searcher sees post-cutoff search results and chooses which URLs are fetched, so page selection can be conditioned on the answer; only the URLs leave the searcher, and in backtests every fetched page is a snapshot dated <= as_of.
Live pages are used only when as_of is today; in backtests every page is an archived snapshot dated <= as_of.
The leak sentinel only catches registered official values in common formats, not paraphrased or derived numbers.
The model's own training data (knowledge cutoff unpublished) can include history before as_of; it cannot include the target if the target was published after the model's release.
Wayback snapshots are captured by a third party; a snapshot date <= as_of proves the content existed by then.
Assumption values are proposed by the judge model from its own knowledge, which can include the target's history before as_of; code checks their form, not where the number came from.
